questions.q: A 28-year-old man presents with a painless ulcer on the glans penis for 10 days. The base is clean, indurated, and the inguinal lymph nodes are rubbery and non-tender. Dark-field microscopy of the ulcer exudate shows motile spiral organisms. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
opts: Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM single dose
Doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 14 days
questions.exp: Primary syphilis caused by Treponema pallidum is treated with benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM as a single dose. This remains the drug of choice per WHO and national guidelines.

questions.q: A 35-year-old farmer presents with multiple hypopigmented anaesthetic patches on the trunk, thickened great auricular nerve, and claw hand deformity of the right hand. Slit-skin smear shows a bacteriological index of 4+. Which WHO classification does this patient fall under?
questions.exp: A bacteriological index ≥2+ (or >5 patches) classifies leprosy as multibacillary (MB). This patient has BI of 4+ and nerve involvement with deformity, confirming MB leprosy requiring 12 months of MDT (rifampicin + dapsone + clofazimine).

questions.q: A 55-year-old woman presents with tense bullae on normal and erythematous skin on the trunk and limbs. Direct immunofluorescence shows linear IgG and C3 deposition along the basement membrane zone. The target antigen is most likely:
questions.exp: Bullous pemphigoid (BP) is characterized by tense bullae and linear IgG/C3 at the BMZ on DIF. The main target antigen is BP180 (BPAG2/type XVII collagen), specifically the NC16A domain. BP230 is also targeted but is less discriminatory.

questions.q: A 22-year-old woman with a 3-year history of discoid lupus erythematosus presents with malar rash, arthralgia, oral ulcers, and proteinuria of 3.5 g/day. ANA is 1:640 (homogeneous), anti-dsDNA is strongly positive. The most appropriate initial treatment for her renal disease is:
questions.exp: This patient has lupus nephritis (nephrotic-range proteinuria). Induction therapy for proliferative lupus nephritis consists of high-dose corticosteroids combined with mycophenolate mofetil (or cyclophosphamide). MMF is preferred for induction in non-severe cases due to comparable efficacy and better tolerability.

questions.q: A 40-year-old man presents with well-defined erythematous plaques with silvery-white scales on elbows, knees, and scalp with nail pitting and onycholysis. His PASI score is 18. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
opts: Biological therapy with a TNF-alpha inhibitor
questions.exp: A PASI score >10 indicates moderate-to-severe psoriasis. Systemic therapy is warranted. Methotrexate is first-line systemic therapy for moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis. Biologics are reserved for failure or contraindication to conventional systemic agents.

questions.q: A 6-year-old child presents with honey-colored crusted lesions around the mouth and nose. Gram stain of the crust shows Gram-positive cocci in clusters. The organism most likely responsible and first-line treatment are:
opts: Staphylococcus aureus; topical mupirocin for localized disease
questions.exp: Non-bullous impetigo is most commonly caused by Staphylococcus aureus (or mixed S. aureus + S. pyogenes). For localized disease, topical mupirocin or retapamulin is first-line. Oral antibiotics (flucloxacillin, cefalexin) are used for extensive disease.

questions.q: A 30-year-old HIV-positive patient (CD4 = 80 cells/μL) presents with extensive white plaques on the tongue that scrape off leaving a bleeding base. KOH mount shows pseudohyphae and budding yeast. The most appropriate treatment is:
opts: Oral fluconazole 200 mg loading dose then 100 mg/day for 14 days
questions.exp: Oropharyngeal candidiasis in an immunocompromised patient (CD4 <200) is treated with systemic azoles. Oral fluconazole is superior to topical agents in HIV patients with low CD4 counts. Amphotericin B is reserved for systemic/refractory candidiasis.

questions.q: A 25-year-old woman presents with grouped vesicles on an erythematous base over the right side of her chest along a dermatomal distribution, preceded by 3 days of burning pain. She is otherwise healthy. The drug of choice and optimal timing of initiation is:
opts: Valacyclovir 1000 mg TID for 7 days, started within 72 hours of rash onset
Acyclovir cream applied 5 times daily for 5 days
Famciclovir 250 mg TID for 5 days, started any time
questions.exp: Herpes zoster (shingles) is treated with oral antivirals ideally within 72 hours of rash onset to reduce severity and duration. Valacyclovir 1000 mg TID × 7 days and famciclovir 500 mg TID × 7 days are preferred over acyclovir due to better bioavailability and simpler dosing.

questions.q: A 45-year-old man presents with a pearly, rolled-edge nodule on the nose that has slowly enlarged over 2 years. Central ulceration is present. Dermoscopy shows arborizing blood vessels and blue-gray ovoid nests. Histology is most likely to show:
opts: Squamous cell carcinoma with keratin pearls
Palisading basal cells with peripheral nuclear retraction and mucinous stroma
Merkel cell carcinoma with small blue cells
questions.exp: Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) classically presents as a pearly nodule with rolled edges and arborizing vessels on dermoscopy. Histology shows islands of basaloid cells with peripheral palisading and retraction artefact from surrounding stroma.

questions.q: A 19-year-old woman presents with periorbital edema, vesiculation, and weeping eczema over both eyelids after starting a new mascara. Patch testing is planned. Which of the following is the most common allergen in cosmetics causing this reaction?
questions.exp: Allergic contact dermatitis from cosmetics commonly involves fragrance mix (the most common cosmetic allergen) and preservatives. Nickel is the most common allergen overall but is not typically found in cosmetics. The eyelid location and mascara exposure point to fragrance or preservative allergy.

questions.q: A 32-year-old woman with systemic sclerosis presents with Raynaud's phenomenon, tight skin limited to hands and face, telangiectasias, calcinosis, and dysphagia. Her anticentromere antibody is positive. What pattern of systemic sclerosis does she have, and which visceral complication is she most at risk for?
opts: Limited cutaneous SSc (CREST); pulmonary arterial hypertension
Diffuse cutaneous SSc; pulmonary arterial hypertension
questions.exp: Anticentromere antibody is associated with limited cutaneous SSc (CREST syndrome). The major visceral complication in limited SSc is pulmonary arterial hypertension, whereas diffuse SSc with anti-Scl-70 is more associated with interstitial lung disease and renal crisis.

questions.q: A 50-year-old patient presents with recurrent episodes of flaccid bullae that rupture easily, leaving extensive erosions on the trunk and oral mucosa. Nikolsky sign is positive. DIF shows intercellular IgG and C3 in the epidermis ('chicken-wire' pattern). The pathogenic antibody targets:
questions.exp: Pemphigus vulgaris is characterized by flaccid bullae, positive Nikolsky sign, and intercellular IgG on DIF (chicken-wire pattern). The pathogenic antibodies target Desmoglein 3 (mucosal type) and both Desmoglein 3 + Desmoglein 1 (mucocutaneous type), disrupting desmosomal adhesion.

questions.q: A 16-year-old girl presents with a 6-month history of hair loss in a well-defined oval patch on the scalp. Dermoscopy shows exclamation mark hairs, yellow dots, and black dots. The most likely diagnosis and first-line treatment for a single patch are:
questions.exp: Alopecia areata presents with well-demarcated patches of hair loss; dermoscopy shows exclamation mark hairs (pathognomonic), yellow dots (empty follicles), and black dots (broken hairs). For limited patchy disease, intralesional triamcinolone acetonide (5-10 mg/mL) is the first-line treatment.

questions.q: A 28-year-old man presents with a shallow genital ulcer with ragged undermined edges, intensely painful, with unilateral tender inguinal lymphadenopathy (bubo). Gram stain of the ulcer shows 'school of fish' pattern. The causative organism is:
questions.exp: Chancroid is caused by Haemophilus ducreyi. It presents with a painful soft ulcer with ragged undermined edges and unilateral tender inguinal bubo. Gram stain shows small Gram-negative rods in 'school of fish' or 'railroad track' pattern. Treatment: azithromycin 1 g single dose or ceftriaxone 250 mg IM.

questions.q: A 4-year-old child presents with a scaly patch on the scalp with bright green fluorescence under Wood's lamp. KOH mount of hair shaft shows small spores outside the hair shaft (ectothrix pattern). The most likely causative organism is:
questions.exp: Microsporum canis causes ectothrix tinea capitis with bright green fluorescence on Wood's lamp (due to pteridine metabolites). Trichophyton species (T. tonsurans, T. violaceum) typically cause endothrix infection without fluorescence. T. schoenleinii causes favus with dull green fluorescence.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman presents with diffuse hyperpigmentation on sun-exposed areas, periorificial hypopigmentation, and oral mucosal pigmentation. Recent history includes fatigue and weight loss. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Addison's disease (primary adrenal insufficiency) causes generalized hyperpigmentation due to elevated ACTH (which cross-reacts with melanocortin receptors), particularly in sun-exposed areas, skin folds, pressure points, and oral mucosa. Constitutional symptoms (fatigue, weight loss) support this diagnosis.

questions.q: A 3-year-old child is brought with pruritic, weeping, crusted plaques on both cheeks and extensor surfaces of limbs since infancy. Serum IgE is markedly elevated. Family history of asthma. The most relevant filaggrin gene mutation affects which skin function?
opts: Epidermal barrier function leading to transepidermal water loss
questions.exp: Atopic dermatitis is strongly associated with loss-of-function mutations in the filaggrin (FLG) gene. Filaggrin is essential for formation of the cornified envelope and the skin barrier. FLG mutations lead to impaired barrier function and increased transepidermal water loss (TEWL), allowing allergen penetration and sensitization.

questions.q: A 60-year-old man presents with an irregularly pigmented lesion on the sole measuring 1.2 cm with variegated colors, irregular borders, and recent ulceration. Dermoscopy shows an irregular blotch and parallel ridge pattern. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Acral lentiginous melanoma (ALM) is the most common subtype of melanoma in dark-skinned individuals and occurs on palms, soles, and nail apparatus. Dermoscopy hallmark on acral skin is the 'parallel ridge pattern' (pigmentation along the ridges, not furrows). Ulceration suggests advanced disease.

questions.q: During liquid nitrogen cryotherapy for a seborrhoeic keratosis on the face, the dermatologist applies the probe for 15 seconds. What is the critical tissue temperature that must be reached to ensure cell death?
questions.exp: Cell death in cryotherapy occurs when tissue temperature reaches -20°C or below. Liquid nitrogen achieves -196°C at the probe tip, but tissue temperature varies with distance. A freeze halo of at least 2-5 mm is targeted for benign lesions, with longer freeze times for malignant lesions.

questions.q: A 38-year-old woman on long-term dapsone therapy for dermatitis herpetiformis presents with jaundice, pallor, and dark urine. Her G6PD level is found to be markedly low. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: G6PD deficiency-related hemolytic anemia triggered by dapsone
questions.exp: Dapsone is an oxidant drug that can trigger hemolytic anemia in patients with G6PD deficiency. G6PD is required to generate NADPH for RBC protection against oxidative stress. Dapsone also causes dose-dependent methemoglobinemia and hemolysis even in G6PD-normal individuals at high doses, but is markedly worse in G6PD deficiency.

questions.q: A 25-year-old man presents with a 3-cm annular plaque with central clearing, raised active border, and fine scaling on the inner thigh and groin. KOH mount shows septate hyphae. The most appropriate topical antifungal is:
questions.exp: Tinea cruris (ringworm of the groin) is caused by dermatophytes (Trichophyton rubrum most commonly). Topical allylamines (terbinafine) or azoles (clotrimazole, miconazole) are first-line. Terbinafine 1% cream for 2 weeks is highly effective. Nystatin is active only against Candida, not dermatophytes.

questions.q: A 70-year-old man presents with a rapidly growing, firm, flesh-colored nodule on the cheek that appeared 6 weeks ago. Histology shows nests of small round cells with scanty cytoplasm, vesicular nuclei, and numerous mitoses, with CK20 dot-like positivity and synaptophysin positivity. The diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Merkel cell carcinoma (MCC) is a rare, aggressive neuroendocrine tumour. Histology shows small round blue cells. The hallmark is CK20 positivity in a 'dot-like' perinuclear pattern and neuroendocrine markers (synaptophysin, chromogranin). CK7 is negative (distinguishing from metastatic SCLC which is CK7+/CK20-).

questions.q: A 30-year-old pregnant woman in her 3rd trimester presents with intensely pruritic urticarial papules and plaques starting in the abdominal striae, sparing the periumbilical area. There are no bullae. The most likely diagnosis is:
opts: Pruritic urticarial papules and plaques of pregnancy (PUPPP)
questions.exp: PUPPP (Polymorphic eruption of pregnancy) characteristically begins in the abdominal striae during the 3rd trimester, spares the periumbilical area, and has no bullae. Pemphigoid gestationis starts at the umbilicus and progresses to bullae, showing linear C3 on DIF.

questions.q: A 42-year-old male patient with psoriasis is started on methotrexate. Which baseline investigation is most important before initiation to monitor for the most serious adverse effect?
opts: Liver function tests and hepatitis B/C serology
questions.exp: Hepatotoxicity (hepatic fibrosis and cirrhosis) is the most serious long-term adverse effect of methotrexate. Baseline LFTs, hepatitis B and C serology are mandatory. Cumulative dose >3.5 g increases fibrosis risk significantly. CBC (for myelosuppression) and renal function are also required.

questions.q: A dermatologist performs a punch biopsy. The punch is rotated at 90° to the relaxed skin tension lines (RSTL). What is the expected shape of the resulting wound?
opts: Oval, with the long axis perpendicular to RSTL
Oval, with the long axis parallel to RSTL
No difference in shape regardless of orientation
questions.exp: When a circular punch is removed from skin, the wound gapes due to skin tension and elongates parallel to the RSTLs (the direction of least resistance). Punching perpendicular to RSTL therefore results in an oval wound oriented parallel to RSTL.

questions.q: A 20-year-old man presents with multiple comedones, papules, nodules, and sinus tracts on the face, chest, and back with scarring. His Acne Global Assessment is severe. The only treatment known to alter the natural history of acne is:
questions.exp: Oral isotretinoin is the only treatment proven to induce long-term remission and alter the natural history of acne. It targets all four pathogenic factors: sebum production, follicular hyperkeratinization, C. acnes colonization, and inflammation. It is indicated for severe nodulocystic/conglobate acne.

questions.q: A 55-year-old woman on hydroxyurea for chronic myeloid leukemia develops painful ulcers on bilateral malleoli and hyperpigmented longitudinal nail bands. These side effects are characteristic of which drug?
questions.exp: Hydroxyurea (hydroxycarbamide) is well known for causing leg ulcers (classically over the malleoli), hyperpigmentation, longitudinal melanonychia (nail banding), and cutaneous features resembling dermatomyositis. These are unique adverse effects not typically seen with other cytotoxics.

questions.q: A 35-year-old man from central India presents with a well-defined hypopigmented plaque on the forearm with complete loss of sensation. Slit-skin smear is negative. The clinician plans to start WHO paucibacillary MDT. The correct regimen for 6 months is:
opts: Rifampicin 600 mg monthly (supervised) + Dapsone 100 mg daily (self-administered)
Rifampicin 600 mg monthly + Clofazimine 300 mg monthly + Dapsone 100 mg daily
Rifampicin 600 mg daily + Clofazimine 50 mg daily
questions.exp: WHO PB-MDT (for ≤5 patches, BI negative) consists of: Rifampicin 600 mg once monthly (supervised) + Dapsone 100 mg daily (self-administered) for 6 months. Clofazimine is added only in MB-MDT. Dapsone monotherapy is obsolete due to resistance.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman presents with a 2-year history of symmetric facial hyperpigmentation over malar areas, forehead, and upper lip. It worsens in summer and after pregnancy. Wood's lamp examination accentuates the pigmentation markedly. This indicates the pigment is located in the:
questions.exp: Melasma can be epidermal (enhanced by Wood's lamp), dermal (no enhancement), or mixed. Wood's lamp accentuation indicates epidermal melasma, as it enhances contrast of epidermal melanin but not dermal melanin. Epidermal type responds better to topical depigmenting agents.

questions.q: A type 1 lepra reaction is seen in a patient on anti-leprosy treatment. He develops sudden acute inflammation of a previously hypopigmented patch with new patches and nerve tenderness. The immediate management is:
opts: Add prednisolone 40-60 mg/day while continuing MDT
questions.exp: Type 1 lepra reaction (reversal reaction) is a delayed-type hypersensitivity reaction occurring in borderline leprosy. Management is prednisolone 40-60 mg/day tapered over 12-24 weeks while CONTINUING MDT (never stop). Thalidomide is used for ENL (type 2) reactions, not type 1.

questions.q: A 22-year-old man presents with grouped papulovesicles over the dorsum of the hands and extensor forearms with intense pruritus. Histology shows neutrophil microabscesses at the dermal papillary tips. DIF shows granular IgA deposits at the dermal papillae. The associated systemic condition is:
questions.exp: Dermatitis herpetiformis (DH) is characterized by intensely pruritic grouped vesicles over extensor surfaces. DIF shows granular IgA at dermal papillary tips (pathognomonic). It is strongly associated with coeliac disease (gluten-sensitive enteropathy). Treatment is dapsone plus a strict gluten-free diet.
